verdict: Caution: lend selectively to powerloom units with confirmed yarn supply and clean receivables; avoid units dependent on Rajasthan processing and handloom-only weavers.
title: Malegaon handloom & powerloom: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
Malegaon runs on powerlooms and handlooms that buy grey yarn, weave fabric, and sell to traders or send cloth to processing units. **Cash is made on the loom, but it is collected after processing and trade margins are thin.** The working-capital cycle is the whole business: yarn must be bought before weaving, and payment comes after fabric is sold. ICRA notes the weaving business is fixed-capital and working-capital intensive, so funding needs are typically high [8], and working capital is driven by inventory holding plus receivables [9]. So when a proposal lands, check the yarn purchase-to-fabric-sale cycle and the receivable days; if receivables stretch beyond the stated trade cycle, ask which buyer and which processing unit sits in between.

## What has broken now
Local reporting says closed processing units in Rajasthan are hitting Malegaon powerlooms hard and forcing unit shutdowns [3], and that the supply crisis runs wider than Rajasthan [2]. **The break is upstream and downstream of the loom, not in the loom itself.** A unit with looms running but no processing outlet is a unit with unsold fabric and stuck cash. So when a proposal lands, check where the borrower's fabric is processed; if the answer is a Rajasthan unit, ask for proof it is running and for alternate processing arrangements.

## Where the growth is
Maharashtra GST collections are running +8.6% Apr-to-date against India +6.1% [D], and India-wide IIP for NIC 13 output is +13.1% YoY with +11.9% Apr-to-date [D]. **The state is collecting faster than the country and textile output is expanding, so there is demand to lend into.** Peer results support the fabric side: Borana Weaves sales rose 42.04% to Rs 111.36 crore in the December 2025 quarter [6] and 27.99% to Rs 100.73 crore in the March 2026 quarter [7]. Pursue powerloom units with their own or tied-up processing, units selling directly to traders with short receivable cycles, and handloom units with design-led buyers — one such organisation grows 10% year-on-year organically with a client base up 30% in the past term [5]. Avoid handloom-only weavers with no buyer contract and units wholly dependent on Rajasthan processing [3].

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the cycle, not the loom count.** ICRA notes low leverage improves financial flexibility in a downturn and keeps fixed financing costs low [10], and that aggressive debt reliance makes entities more vulnerable to cyclical downturns [8]. So when a proposal lands, size the term loan to the borrower's own equity and keep the working-capital limit tied to the actual yarn-to-fabric cycle; if leverage is already high, ask for promoter contribution before sanction. Take stock and receivable statements every month, and a processing-unit confirmation every quarter.

## Early-warning signs
- Loom utilisation falling below the borrower's own stated norm (monthly) -> ask for the buyer order book and freeze fresh limits.
- Receivable days stretching beyond the stated trade cycle (monthly) -> ask which buyer and which processing unit, and seek direct confirmation.
- Yarn purchase shifting to costlier spot buying (monthly) -> ask for the supply contract and rework the drawing power.
- Any news of further Rajasthan processing closures (ongoing) -> ask for alternate processing proof before renewing [3].
- GST payment delays or falling turnover versus the state's +8.6% [D] (monthly) -> ask for sales register and reassess the limit.
